stem: A 78-year-old man lives alone and for a month has eaten little besides crackers and coffee. He has lost 7 kg, has a BMI of 19, and has weakness with visible muscle wasting. Blood is drawn to measure several hormones.
oneliner: 78M + a month of crackers and coffee + 7-kg loss + muscle wasting → which hormone is raised?
ask: Which hormone level is most likely increased?

whyNot.A: Insulin **falls** with little carbohydrate intake and low glucose
whyNot.B: IGF-1 depends on adequate nutrition and **falls** in starvation, even though GH rises
whyNot.C: Gonadal axis is **suppressed** in starvation; testosterone falls
whyNot.D: Peripheral T3 **drops** as conversion shifts to reverse T3 to save energy

why: Prolonged starvation switches the body to fuel-sparing mode: **cortisol** (and GH) rise to drive gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and **muscle protein breakdown**, which causes wasting and **negative nitrogen balance**. Insulin, IGF-1, T3 and testosterone all fall.
chain: Weeks of minimal intake lower glucose and insulin
Muscle protein is broken down for amino acids
Nitrogen balance turns negative; IGF-1, T3 and testosterone fall

idea.rule: Starvation: counter-regulatory hormones (cortisol, GH, glucagon) up; anabolic and metabolic-rate hormones down.
also: Cortisol-driven proteolysis supplies amino acids for gluconeogenesis
IGF-1 is a marker of nutritional status
Low T3 with raised reverse T3 occurs in fasting and critical illness
Anorexia nervosa shows the same hormone pattern

stem: A 25-year-old man has eaten nothing for seven days while stranded in the desert, though he drank water. Liver enzyme activity is measured on his arrival at hospital.
oneliner: 25M + 1 week without food, water only → hepatic enzyme changes?
ask: Which pattern of hepatic changes is expected?

whyNot.A: That is the **fed pattern**; after a week without food insulin is low and glucagon high
whyNot.B: After a week without food the liver must make glucose, so **glucose-6-phosphatase and PEPCK rise**, not fall
whyNot.C: After a week without food **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate falls** and **PEPCK rises**; this set has both the wrong way
whyNot.D: PEPCK and G6Pase do rise, but a week without food **lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and pyruvate kinase activity**

answer: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate down, glucose-6-phosphatase up, PEPCK up, pyruvate kinase down
why: Prolonged fasting means **high glucagon, low insulin** and active **protein kinase A**. PKA lowers **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate** and **inactivates pyruvate kinase**, so glycolysis shuts down, while **glucose-6-phosphatase and PEPCK** are induced to favor gluconeogenesis.
chain: Week without food: insulin falls, glucagon rises
cAMP and protein kinase A become active
PKA phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2, so fructose 2,6-bisphosphate falls
PKA phosphorylates and inactivates pyruvate kinase, slowing glycolysis
Gene induction raises PEPCK and glucose-6-phosphatase, so the liver makes glucose

idea.rule: In fasting the liver switches off glycolysis and switches on gluconeogenesis.
also: Glucagon phosphorylates and inactivates liver pyruvate kinase
Low fructose 2,6-bisphosphate removes PFK-1 activation and frees FBPase-1
Cortisol also induces PEPCK and G6Pase
Insulin does the reverse

stem: Isolated hepatocytes are incubated with glucagon. Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate level, PFK-1 activity and FBPase-2 activity are measured and compared with untreated cells.
oneliner: Hepatocytes + glucagon → F2,6BP, PFK-1, FBPase-2?
ask: Which pattern of change is expected after glucagon?

whyNot.A: This is the **insulin response**; glucagon pushes the bifunctional enzyme the other way
whyNot.C: A fall in **fructose 2,6-bisphosphate** cannot increase PFK-1 activity, since it is PFK-1's activator
whyNot.D: A **raised fructose 2,6-bisphosphate** would activate PFK-1, not lower it, and cannot follow glucagon
whyNot.E: If **FBPase-2 activity fell**, fructose 2,6-bisphosphate would not fall

answer: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate down, PFK-1 activity down, FBPase-2 activity up
why: Glucagon raises cAMP and **PKA phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme**, which **turns on FBPase-2** and turns off PFK-2. **Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate falls**, losing its activation of **PFK-1**, so glycolysis slows and gluconeogenesis is favored.
chain: Glucagon binds its liver receptor, cAMP rises
FBPase-2 domain active, PFK-2 domain off, so fructose 2,6-bisphosphate falls
PFK-1 loses its activator, glycolysis slows, gluconeogenesis rises

idea.rule: Glucagon phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme to lower fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; insulin dephosphorylates it to raise it.
also: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1
Insulin: PFK-2 active, F2,6BP up, glycolysis up
Epinephrine acts through cAMP in liver the same way as glucagon
In liver, phosphorylation of metabolic enzymes generally signals the fasting state

stem: A liver cytosol extract is incubated with fructose 6-phosphate and ATP. A TCA cycle intermediate that builds up when the cell has abundant fuel is then added, and PFK-1 activity falls.
oneliner: Liver extract + F6P + ATP, then a TCA intermediate that builds up with plenty of fuel → PFK-1 falls. Which one?
ask: Which added molecule most likely decreased PFK-1 activity?

whyNot.B: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent **activator** of PFK-1
whyNot.C: ADP, like AMP, signals **low energy** and does not inhibit
whyNot.E: Fructose 6-phosphate is the **substrate**; more of it raises the rate

why: PFK-1 is **inhibited by ATP and citrate** and activated by **AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate**. **Citrate** exported from mitochondria means fuel is plentiful, so it **slows glycolysis** at its rate-limiting step.
chain: Mitochondria have plentiful fuel and high ATP
Citrate binds PFK-1 and enhances ATP inhibition
Glycolysis slows while citrate feeds fatty acid synthesis

idea.rule: PFK-1 is inhibited by high energy signals (ATP, citrate) and activated by low energy signals (AMP) and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
also: Citrate also activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by ATP and alanine
Hexokinase is inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate
PFK-1 is the rate-limiting step of glycolysis

stem: A 27-year-old woman eats a carbohydrate-rich lunch and, two hours later, drinks a sugar-sweetened cola. Her insulin is high and glucagon is low.
oneliner: 27F + carb lunch then sugary cola 2 h later, insulin high → which hepatic enzyme activity rises?
ask: Which hepatic enzyme activity is increased?

whyNot.A: CPT-I is **inhibited by malonyl-CoA** in the fed state, so fat oxidation falls
whyNot.B: Insulin **dephosphorylates** and turns off glycogen phosphorylase in the fed state
whyNot.D: PEPCK is induced by **fasting** and glucagon, not by high insulin
whyNot.E: PKA needs **cAMP from glucagon**, which is low in this woman

why: After a carbohydrate meal, **insulin is high**, so **acetyl-CoA carboxylase** is dephosphorylated and active, making **malonyl-CoA** for fatty acid synthesis. Malonyl-CoA **blocks CPT-I**, while gluconeogenic and glycogenolytic enzymes are shut off.
chain: Carbohydrate meal: insulin rises, glucagon falls
cAMP and PKA fall; enzymes are dephosphorylated
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I so fat is not burned
Fatty acid synthesis rises, PEPCK and glycogen phosphorylase fall

idea.rule: Insulin makes the liver store energy: fatty acid synthesis on, fat oxidation and glucose output off.
also: Insulin also induces fatty acid synthase
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, preventing futile cycling
Insulin lowers cAMP and PKA activity
Glycogen synthase is active when dephosphorylated

stem: A healthy 30-year-old man has taken only water for 2 days. His liver glycogen is nearly used up. Glucagon and cortisol are high, and his liver is taking up alanine, lactate and glycerol.
oneliner: 30M + water-only fast day 2 + liver glycogen nearly gone + high glucagon and cortisol + liver takes up alanine, lactate, glycerol → main source of blood glucose?
ask: Which process now mainly maintains his blood glucose?

whyNot.A: **Liver glycogen is nearly used up**, so this store is spent
whyNot.B: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and **cannot release glucose**; the substrates are going into the liver
whyNot.D: Ketones are a fuel for tissues; they **cannot be turned back into glucose**
whyNot.E: He is on **water only**, so nothing is being absorbed

why: After about 24 hours **liver glycogen runs out** and the liver switches to making new glucose from **amino acids, lactate and glycerol**. High **glucagon and cortisol** drive this switch.
chain: Liver converts amino acids, lactate, glycerol to glucose
Gluconeogenesis becomes the main glucose source

idea.rule: Fasting glucose: glycogenolysis for roughly the first day, then gluconeogenesis.
also: Glycerol from adipose lipolysis feeds gluconeogenesis
Alanine from muscle (glucose-alanine cycle)
Lactate from the Cori cycle
Only the liver (and kidney in long fasts) can release free glucose

stem: A 10-year-old girl has vomited for 2 weeks and taken almost nothing by mouth. She is thin with visible muscle wasting. Glucose is 30 mg/dL, bicarbonate is low, and urine ketones are 4+.
oneliner: 10F + 2 weeks vomiting + muscle wasting + glucose 30 + low bicarbonate + urine ketones 4+ → what is her brain mainly burning?
ask: Which fuel is her brain now using for much of its energy?

whyNot.B: Bound to albumin and **do not cross the blood-brain barrier** well; the liver converts them to the ketones in her urine
whyNot.C: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, and her **glucose is only 30 mg/dL**
whyNot.D: Made from glucose and recycled by the Cori cycle, so it gives **no net new fuel** in prolonged starvation
whyNot.E: Used by the liver for gluconeogenesis; the **4+ ketones** show the fuel that spares her muscle protein

why: In prolonged starvation the liver oxidizes fatty acids to **acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate**. The brain adapts to use these, so it needs **less glucose** and the body breaks down **less muscle protein**. Ketoacids also explain the **low bicarbonate**.
chain: Acetyl-CoA is made into ketone bodies
Less glucose needed, so less muscle protein is spent

idea.rule: In prolonged fasting the brain shifts from glucose to ketones.
also: Red cells always depend on glucose (no mitochondria)
Liver makes ketones but cannot use them (lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase)
Ketoacidosis lowers bicarbonate with a raised anion gap
Starvation ketosis is milder than diabetic ketoacidosis

stem: A 3-month-old boy has fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and ketosis after missed feeds, and his liver is mildly enlarged. During testing, his blood glucose did not rise after IV glycerol or after IV fructose.
oneliner: 3mo M + fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + ketosis + mild hepatomegaly + no glucose rise after glycerol or fructose → which substrate still raises glucose?
ask: Which of the following would still raise his blood glucose?

whyNot.A: His glucose **did not rise** after glycerol
whyNot.B: His glucose **did not rise** after fructose
whyNot.C: Enters through pyruvate, **above the block** that stopped glycerol and fructose; his lactate is already high
whyNot.D: Already **elevated in his blood**, because it cannot reach glucose past the block

why: Glycerol, fructose, alanine and lactate all pass through **fructose-1,6-bisphosphate**, so a block at **fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase** stops them. **Galactose** enters as **glucose-1-phosphate** and joins below that step.
chain: Substrates entering above it back up (lactate, alanine, glycerol)
It bypasses the block and raises glucose

idea.rule: A block in gluconeogenesis stops only substrates that enter above it.
also: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency blocks glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so even galactose fails
Fasting hypoglycemia plus lactic acidosis points to a gluconeogenic block
Glycerol enters as DHAP, above FBPase-1
Fructose enters via fructose-1-phosphate to triose phosphates

stem: Liver mitochondria from a fasted rat are given palmitate. The rate at which a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate rises sharply, through direct allosteric activation by a product of palmitate breakdown.
oneliner: Fasted rat liver mitochondria + palmitate + biotin-dependent pyruvate-to-oxaloacetate step speeds up + allosteric activation by a palmitate breakdown product → which activator?
ask: Which molecule directly activates that enzyme?

whyNot.A: A hormone that cannot act on **isolated mitochondria**, and it is **low in fasting**
whyNot.C: Activates **acetyl-CoA carboxylase** for fat synthesis; it is not a product of **palmitate breakdown** itself
whyNot.D: A **cytosolic glycolytic** signal that activates phosphofructokinase-1, absent from **isolated mitochondria**
whyNot.E: A low-energy signal; **palmitate oxidation** is supplying ATP, so AMP is low

why: **Pyruvate carboxylase** needs **biotin** and is switched on by **acetyl-CoA**. In fasting, fatty acid oxidation raises acetyl-CoA, which sends pyruvate to **oxaloacetate** for gluconeogenesis rather than into the TCA cycle.
chain: PDH is inhibited, so pyruvate is saved for gluconeogenesis

idea.rule: Plenty of acetyl-CoA tells the cell to make glucose, not burn more pyruvate.
also: Acetyl-CoA inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase
Biotin is also a cofactor for acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Avidin in raw egg white blocks biotin
Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency causes lactic acidosis

stem: A 2-week-old boy feeds poorly and vomits, and his urine smells of maple syrup. Blood leucine, isoleucine and valine and their ketoacids are high. These levels fall when he is given a high dose of a vitamin supplement.
oneliner: 2wk M + poor feeding + maple-syrup urine odor + high leucine, isoleucine, valine and ketoacids + falls on high-dose vitamin → which cofactor?
ask: Which cofactor of the defective enzyme does the supplement supply?

whyNot.A: Used by **carboxylases**; this enzyme **removes** a carboxyl group from ketoacids
whyNot.B: Used by **transaminases**; the **ketoacids are high**, so the transamination step is working
whyNot.C: Needed for **hydroxylation** (collagen), not oxidative decarboxylation of ketoacids
whyNot.E: Needed for **gamma-carboxylation** of clotting factors, unrelated to this defect

why: The **branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase** does **oxidative decarboxylation** and needs **thiamine pyrophosphate**. Some MSUD patients respond to **high-dose thiamine**.
chain: Ketoacids of leucine, isoleucine, valine accumulate
TPP supplement raises residual enzyme activity in responsive cases

idea.rule: Thiamine pyrophosphate serves enzymes that decarboxylate alpha-ketoacids and the transketolase reaction.
also: Pyruvate dehydrogenase
Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway
Thiamine deficiency (beriberi, Wernicke) raises pyruvate and lactate

stem: A 6-month-old boy has had hypoglycemia without ketones during a viral illness, and an enlarged heart. Testing shows long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. His diet is changed so that a different fat supplies his energy.
oneliner: 6mo M + hypoketotic hypoglycemia + cardiomyopathy + long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency → which fat supplies energy despite the block?
ask: Which dietary fat should supply his energy?

whyNot.B: Their fatty acids **need the carnitine shuttle** and the blocked long-chain step
whyNot.C: A **long-chain** (16-carbon) fatty acid, so it meets the same block
whyNot.D: Shortened only slowly in **peroxisomes** and not a usable bulk fuel; they build up in adrenoleukodystrophy
whyNot.E: A **branched** fatty acid handled by peroxisomal alpha-oxidation, not an energy rescue here

why: **Medium-chain fatty acids** enter mitochondria **without carnitine** and are oxidized by medium-chain enzymes, so they **bypass the long-chain block**. In the defect, long-chain acylcarnitines pile up and ketones stay low.
chain: MCT enters mitochondria without CPT-I or carnitine
Medium-chain oxidation supplies acetyl-CoA and energy

idea.rule: Medium-chain fats skip the carnitine shuttle and the long-chain enzymes.
also: Carnitine deficiency also gives hypoketotic hypoglycemia
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency is the commonest FAO defect
Avoid fasting in fatty acid oxidation defects
CPT-I is the rate-limiting step for long-chain entry

stem: A newborn girl is lethargic with ammonia 6 times normal and brittle, easily broken hair shafts. Her urine contains large amounts of argininosuccinate.
oneliner: Newborn F + lethargy + ammonia ×6 + brittle hair (trichorrhexis nodosa) + urinary argininosuccinate → which other metabolite is raised?
ask: Which other metabolite is most likely raised in her blood?

whyNot.A: A **product** of the lyase step, so it is not made from the **argininosuccinate** piling up in her urine
whyNot.B: Made by the lyase, **downstream** of the block, so it falls
whyNot.C: The cycle's **end product**, low when the cycle is blocked
whyNot.D: Regenerated from arginine, **downstream** of the block, so it is not raised

why: **Argininosuccinate lyase** splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. A block raises **ammonia, citrulline and argininosuccinate** upstream and lowers **arginine** downstream.
chain: Argininosuccinate accumulates in blood and urine
Ammonia rises; brittle hair as arginine becomes limiting

idea.rule: In a urea cycle block, substrates before the block rise and products after it fall.
also: OTC deficiency: orotic acid up, citrulline low
Citrullinemia (argininosuccinate synthetase): citrulline very high
Arginase deficiency: arginine high
Hyperammonemia gives lethargy, vomiting and cerebral edema

stem: A 25-year-old East Asian man flushes and has a fast heart rate after a small drink, and acetaldehyde builds up in his blood. His mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase has a Km for NAD+ of 5600 µM and a kcat of 95 per minute, compared with 37 µM and 180 per minute for the usual enzyme.
oneliner: 25M East Asian + flushing and tachycardia after small alcohol + Km NAD+ 5600 vs 37 µM + kcat 95 vs 180/min + acetaldehyde accumulation → kinetic change?
ask: Which change in the variant enzyme best explains his reaction?

options.A: Tighter NAD+ binding and slower turnover
options.B: Weaker NAD+ binding and faster turnover
options.C: Weaker NAD+ binding and slower turnover
options.D: Tighter NAD+ binding and faster turnover

whyNot.A: A **Km of 5600 versus 37 µM** means weaker, not tighter, binding
whyNot.B: His **kcat is 95 versus 180 per minute**, so turnover is slower
whyNot.D: **Km is higher and kcat is lower**, so both parts are reversed
whyNot.E: The constants given are for **aldehyde dehydrogenase**; they explain the acetaldehyde build-up without any change in ADH

answer: Higher Km for NAD+ and lower kcat, so kcat/Km falls
why: The **ALDH2 variant** binds NAD+ poorly (**Km up**) and turns over slowly (**kcat down**), so **kcat/Km falls** and **acetaldehyde accumulates**, causing flushing and tachycardia.
chain: ALDH2 variant has weaker NAD+ binding

idea.rule: Higher Km means lower affinity; lower kcat means slower turnover; efficiency is kcat/Km.
also: Disulfiram blocks acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, giving the same flushing
Increased acetaldehyde raises esophageal cancer risk
ADH oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde in the cytosol
ALDH2 acts in mitochondria

stem: Reaction velocity is plotted against substrate concentration for a regulatory enzyme, with and without a modifier. With the modifier, the curve is displaced to the right but reaches the same plateau.
oneliner: Velocity vs substrate curve + modifier displaces curve right + same plateau → effect on the enzyme?
ask: What does the modifier do?

options.A: Lowers Vmax while Km stays the same
options.B: Raises Vmax while Km stays the same
options.C: Lowers Km while Vmax stays the same
options.D: Raises Km while Vmax stays the same

whyNot.A: The **plateau is unchanged**, so Vmax has not fallen
whyNot.B: The plateau is **at the same height**, so Vmax has not risen
whyNot.C: A **left** shift would lower Km; this shift is to the **right**
whyNot.E: The **plateau is unchanged** and the shift is to the **right**, not the left

why: A **right shift** means a higher substrate concentration is needed for half-maximal velocity: **Km rises** and **affinity falls**. The **same plateau** means **Vmax is unchanged**.
chain: Half-maximal point moves to higher substrate
Plateau unchanged, so Vmax is the same

idea.rule: Right shift with same plateau: Km up, Vmax same. Left shift: Km down.
also: Competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km with Vmax unchanged
Noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax with Km unchanged
More enzyme raises Vmax
Allosteric activators of regulatory enzymes can lower Km

stem: An extract from resting skeletal muscle has high ATP, low AMP and low calcium, and its hexose phosphates are high. Glycogen breakdown in the extract is very slow.
oneliner: Resting muscle extract + high ATP + low AMP + low calcium + high hexose phosphates + slow glycogen breakdown → which molecule inhibits glycogen phosphorylase?
ask: Which of the following inhibits glycogen phosphorylase in this extract?

whyNot.A: An **activator** that signals low energy, and it is **low** here
whyNot.C: Activates phosphorylase kinase during contraction, and **calcium is low** here
whyNot.D: A hormone that acts on intact cells through **cAMP** to activate the enzyme; not a direct inhibitor in an **extract**
whyNot.E: A **substrate** of phosphorolysis, which would favour breakdown

why: Muscle phosphorylase is **activated by AMP** and **inhibited by ATP and glucose-6-phosphate**. At rest with high energy charge, glycogenolysis is **slowed**.
chain: AMP is low, so no activation

idea.rule: Phosphorylase is on when the cell is low on energy and off when it is full.
also: Exercise raises AMP and Ca2+, activating glycogenolysis
Liver phosphorylase is inhibited by glucose
McArdle disease lacks muscle phosphorylase
Epinephrine activates it via cAMP and PKA

stem: A 25-year-old woman does repeated 200-m sprints and her legs begin to burn and cramp. Her muscles' oxygen supply cannot keep up with demand.
oneliner: 25F + repeated 200-m sprints + burning, cramping legs + oxygen supply short of demand → which process explains the symptoms?
ask: Which process best explains her symptoms?

options.A: Pyruvate reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+
options.B: More oxygen delivery raising muscle acid
options.D: More pyruvate dehydrogenase flux raising muscle acid

whyNot.B: Her problem is **limited** oxygen supply, not more of it
whyNot.C: Beta-oxidation needs **oxygen** and is not the quick response during a sprint
whyNot.D: Needs **oxygen** through the TCA cycle, which is limited here
whyNot.E: This reaction **consumes protons** and buffers acid; it does not cause it

why: When oxygen is short, the electron transport chain cannot reoxidize NADH, so **lactate dehydrogenase** converts **pyruvate to lactate** and regenerates **NAD+** so glycolysis can continue. The **lactic acid** lowers muscle pH and causes burning.
chain: Oxygen supply falls short of demand
Lactate and H+ accumulate: burning, cramps

idea.rule: Lactate production keeps glycolysis going when mitochondria cannot reoxidize NADH.
also: Red cells always make lactate (no mitochondria)
Cori cycle returns lactate to the liver
Lactic acidosis in shock or mitochondrial disease
Thiamine deficiency also raises lactate

note: Plan distractor 'decreased sodium-proton antiporter activity' replaced with a cleaner wrong option, since reduced H+ extrusion would worsen acidosis

stem: Two fuels with the same number of carbon atoms are completely oxidized aerobically. The fat yields much more ATP than the carbohydrate.
oneliner: Two fuels, equal carbon count, both fully oxidized + fat gives far more ATP than carbohydrate → which chemical feature explains it?
ask: Which chemical feature gives the higher ATP yield?

whyNot.A: Oxygen means the carbons are **already partly oxidized**, with less reducing power to release
whyNot.B: Keto carbons are **oxidized** carbons, which carry less reducing power
whyNot.C: Aldehyde carbons are also **oxidized** carbons, carrying less reducing power
whyNot.E: Nitrogen is removed as **urea** and does not supply NADH or FADH2

answer: More hydrogen per carbon (a more reduced fuel)
why: A fuel with **more hydrogen per carbon** has more **reducing equivalents** to pass to **NADH and FADH2**, so its complete oxidation yields **more ATP**. This is why **fat gives more energy per carbon** than carbohydrate.
chain: Fuel is rich in C–H bonds
More NADH and FADH2 are made

idea.rule: The more reduced the carbon, the more ATP its oxidation yields.
also: Fat gives about 9 kcal/g versus 4 kcal/g for carbohydrate
Palmitate gives far more ATP than glucose per molecule
Ethanol (about 7 kcal/g) sits between
Fully oxidized CO2 yields nothing

stem: A 70-year-old woman has eaten almost no protein for months. She has temporal muscle wasting, pitting edema and serum albumin of 2.0 g/dL.
oneliner: 70F + months of almost no protein + temporal wasting + pitting edema + albumin 2.0 → what is her nitrogen balance?
ask: Which best describes her nitrogen balance?

options.D: Positive: body protein is being built up
options.E: Equilibrium: body protein stores are stable

whyNot.A: Her **wasting and low albumin** show net protein loss
whyNot.C: **Muscle wasting** means body protein is being spent
whyNot.D: Her **temporal muscle wasting** shows body protein falling, not rising
whyNot.E: **Low albumin and muscle wasting** show protein stores are shrinking

why: With too little protein (or a diet missing an essential amino acid) the body breaks down its own protein, so **nitrogen excretion exceeds intake**. **Muscle wasting and low albumin** reflect the falling protein stores, and the low albumin causes **edema**.
chain: Body protein is broken down for amino acids

idea.rule: Negative nitrogen balance is net protein loss; positive is net protein gain.
also: Positive: growth, pregnancy, recovery from illness
Negative: severe burns, trauma, sepsis, kwashiorkor
A single missing essential amino acid also causes negative balance
Kwashiorkor: edema from low albumin

stem: A purified enzyme combines PRPP with glutamine to make 5-phosphoribosylamine, the committed step of purine synthesis. Different nucleotides are added to the enzyme at high concentration in separate tubes to see which lower its activity.
oneliner: Purified enzyme PRPP + glutamine to 5-phosphoribosylamine + committed step of purine synthesis + nucleotides added at high concentration → which inhibit it?
ask: Which group of compounds most likely inhibits this enzyme?

whyNot.A: Pyrimidine products, which regulate **carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II**, not this purine step
whyNot.B: Supply one-carbon units to **later** purine steps, not feedback on this one
whyNot.D: Precursors of **PRPP** and not inhibitors of its use
whyNot.E: A **pyrimidine** precursor made by a different enzyme

why: **PRPP amidotransferase** is the **committed step** of purine synthesis and is **feedback inhibited by IMP, AMP and GMP**. Pyrimidine synthesis is instead regulated at **CPS II**.
chain: IMP, AMP, GMP bind the enzyme

idea.rule: Pathway end products inhibit the committed step.
also: CPS II is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP in pyrimidine synthesis
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan) raises PRPP and purine synthesis
Hydroxyurea and mycophenolate act on other nucleotide steps
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase

stem: Cultured chondrocytes are fed different labelled amino acids, and the label is traced into the glucosamine of proteoglycans. The enzyme that first converts fructose 6-phosphate to glucosamine 6-phosphate takes the nitrogen from the amide group of its amino acid donor.
oneliner: Chondrocytes + labelled amino acids traced into proteoglycan glucosamine + enzyme turns fructose-6-phosphate to glucosamine-6-phosphate using an amide nitrogen → which donor?
ask: Which amino acid donates the nitrogen?

whyNot.A: Donates nitrogen in the **urea cycle and nucleotide synthesis**, via its alpha-amino group, not an amide
whyNot.B: Supplies **carbon and nitrogen to the purine ring**, but has no amide group
whyNot.C: Carries nitrogen by **transamination**, using its alpha-amino group, not an amide
whyNot.D: Gives **one-carbon units**; it has no amide nitrogen

shifts.var: Label in glucosamine from amide-labelled glutamine
Label in glucosamine from the other amino acids

why: **Glutamine:fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase** moves the **amide nitrogen of glutamine** to fructose 6-phosphate in the **rate-limiting** step of hexosamine synthesis. The glucosamine goes on to build **glycosaminoglycans**.

idea.rule: Glutamine is the body's amide-nitrogen donor for biosynthesis.
also: Glutamine donates nitrogen in purine and pyrimidine synthesis
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II uses glutamine
Asparagine synthetase takes the amide nitrogen of glutamine
Glutamine carries ammonia safely between tissues
